title: Flyers Winless in Nine, and the Chances Say It's Real
dek: Philadelphia sits 30th with three points, and a 37.1% share of expected goals puts the problem in the play, not in bad luck.
text:
## The record and what's under it

The Flyers are 0-6-3 through nine games, good for 3 points and 30th in the league by points. Three of the losses came past regulation (two in overtime, one in a shootout), which is where those points came from. Everything else has been a regulation loss, and several have been lopsided: 0-7 to PIT in the opener, 1-5 at BOS, 1-4 against CAR and 1-4 at TBL.

The goal totals are 11 scored and 32 allowed. One caution before we go on: the data's streak summary says the Flyers have been outscored 33-11, but the season goal totals say 32 against, and the two don't match. This piece uses 32 and a goal difference of -21, which fits with 11 for.

The short sample matters. Nine games is not a season, and a team can look this bad for a month and recover. But the question for a slump like this is whether the numbers say bad luck or bad play, and here they lean hard toward bad play.

## How the games were played

Philadelphia has 20 expected goals for and 34 against, a 37.1% share of the expected goals. That ranks 32nd in the league. Share of expected goals is the cleanest single measure of who is creating the better chances, and a team below 40% is being outplayed most nights. At five-on-five, the share drops to 35%, so it isn't just penalty trouble pulling the number down.

The game log backs that up. In seven of the nine games, the Flyers' own chance quality made them the less likely winner by a wide margin. By deserved-to-win percentage (the share of simulated replays of every shot that the team wins), they sat at 11% against PIT, 14% at NJD, 22% against CAR in the first meeting, 16% at TBL, 19% at BOS and 21% against CAR in the second. They created 1.55 expected goals against PIT while allowing 4.29. At TBL it was 1.85 against 5.12.

Only two games went the other way. The 1-2 loss at OTT was the Flyers' best performance: 3.39 expected goals to 2.27, a 70% deserved-to-win mark, and they still lost. The 2-3 shootout loss to SEA was close to even at 3.13 to 2.84 (55%). Those two games are the best evidence that the team is capable of better than its record, but two games out of nine is not a trend.

## Finishing, goaltending and why the goal difference is worse than the chances

Here is the part that pulls the record down further. The goal difference of -21 is worse than the -14.0 the chances alone would predict. The gap is finishing: the Flyers have scored 9.0 fewer goals than their shots should have produced. That's a big miss over nine games, and it's the closest thing to bad luck in the profile. Some of it should come back, because finishing tends to drift toward the average over time.

Goaltending, meanwhile, has not been the problem on the whole. The team's goalies have saved 2 goals above expected, so the 32 goals against came from allowing a lot of good chances (34 expected goals against) and not from soft saves. That's an important distinction. If the goalies were the issue, the fix would be personnel. Because the issue is volume and quality of chances allowed, the fix is how the team plays in front of them.

Within that, the two goalies have had different stretches. Joseph Woll has a .916 save percentage with 4.32 goals saved above expected in five starts, even though the team is 0-3-2 in them. He has been better than his results look, including .916 against hard shots over his last five starts. Dan Vladar is at .875 with -2.56 goals saved above expected in four starts. Last season's numbers point the opposite way for each: Woll was at -7.44 and Vladar at +12.74. That's a reminder that goalie numbers swing a lot from year to year and a small sample says little by itself.

## Special teams and discipline

The power play is not carrying anything. It generates 0.55 expected goals per game, ranking 23rd. The penalty kill allows 0.72 expected goals per game, ranking 21st. Both are below average, so neither unit is rescuing the team from its five-on-five problems.

Discipline adds to it. The Flyers take 4.67 penalties per game and draw 3.56, so they give opponents more than one extra power play every night. Combined with a bottom-third penalty kill, that gap hands opponents extra chances the team can't afford.

## The players

The top of the scoring list is thin. Matvei Michkov leads with 3 goals and 3 points, and he has produced 2.39 expected goals of his own, so his 3 goals are 0.61 above what his chances suggest. Christian Dvorak has 2 goals and 3 points against 1.2 expected, which is 0.8 above. Travis Sanheim has 3 points from the blue line while playing 25:23 a night, and the team's share of the play is 11.38 percentage points better with him on the ice. Travis Konecny has 3 points in only 5 games.

The cold side matters more. Tyson Foerster has 2.22 expected goals but 1 goal, which is 1.22 below what his chances call for. Trevor Zegras has 1.94 expected goals and 1 goal, 0.94 under, and the team's share of the play is 10.35 points worse when he's on the ice. Owen Tippett has 1 goal against 1.48 expected. Foerster's drought is the kind that tends to turn on its own.

Two players are in a real dip, not a lucky one. Noah Cates is down to 4.0 on-ice expected goals against a usual 5.5, and his ice time has dropped 3:34 a night. Jamie Drysdale is at 7.4 against a usual 10.0. In both cases the chances have dried up, so waiting for luck won't fix it.

On the positive side, a few players are making the team better when they play. Oliver Bonk (20.83 points better, in 3 games), Cates (19.87) and Porter Martone (13.3) all show a big lift in the team's share of the play. Bonk's sample is only 3 games, so that one is the least certain.

## Will it hold?

Partly. The finishing gap of -9.0 should shrink, and that alone would lift the goal difference. But a 37.1% share of expected goals, ranked 32nd and with 35% at five-on-five, describes a team that is being outplayed, and finishing luck can't cover that for long. Even if the shooting recovers, a team creating 20 expected goals while allowing 34 projects to lose more than it wins. The record is somewhat worse than the play, but the play isn't good.

## What to watch

First, whether the five-on-five share climbs back toward 45%, which would signal real change. Second, the penalty gap: 4.67 taken against 3.56 drawn has to narrow. Third, Zegras and Foerster, whose chances haven't turned into goals. And fourth, how the team handles Woll and Vladar, since Woll's underlying numbers are stronger than his results.
